speechtext:
As a matter of fact, during several months last summer the press of this country gave more publicity to the provincial leader of the C.C.F. in British Columbia than to either Mr. Bracken or to the premier of that province. Actually it will be found that the press of this country is constantly keeping the C.C.F. before the public. Look over the reoords of Hansard for this session and you will find that the same hon. gentlemen who have criticized the CH.C. for publicizing the C.C.F. have done very little else during this session but publicize the C.C.F. You will find pages and pages of Hansard devoted to nothing but to publicizing the C.C.F. party. So that you cannot blame the C.B.C. for publicizing a party that is so much in the news to-day.
I should like. to compliment the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, not upon the publicity they have given to the C.C.F., but upon the good work they have done in helping the Canadian people to appreciate the finer things of life. During this war the C.B.C. have struggled against numerous obstacles and the difficulty of securing good talent in war time. I think they have done a remarkable job in maintaining the morale of the people and giving us an opportunity of appreciating some of the best in literature, art and music and in the discussion of public and social affairs. I compliment the corporation upon that good work.
There are one or two points I should like to call to the attention of the committee before I take my seat. They are not serious. I found last summer, while in New Brunswick, considerable criticism of the, fact that a great many people there 'who were paying licence fees to the broadcasting corporation were unable to get the broadcasting station at Sackville. My information, gathered from radio engineers, some of them employed at that station, is that because of the land area of the maritimes it is practically impossible for one high-powered station to cover that territory adequately, and consequently there are a great many people living in parts of New Brunswick who find it difficult to get that station.
My attention has been called by a number of correspondents to the fact that some of the privately owned stations which have been changing hands during the past few years have in reality been coming under the ownership of private chains contrary to the act. Theoretically these stations are supposed to be
Radio Broadcasting Committee

privately owned; actually, I am told, a considerable number of them are in reality owned by the same interests. I am quite confident that the committee will look into this matter.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
The setting up of this committee to-day for the purpose of inquiring into the activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is but an implementation of recommendations which were made by the committee last year and the year before. I am sure that, in taking the course which they have, the government are taking a course which will renew the confidence which the people of Canada have, and which the parliament of this country should have, in this great public utility.
The criticism which we have heard this afternoon and this evening with reference to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has been mostly of a destructive nature. Criticism, we all agree, can be of two kinds; it can be either constructive or destructive. So far I have not heard from those who would criticize the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation many suggestions which, if put into operation, would tend to make that body better or to have more of the confidence of the Canadian people.
I am not disturbed about the place of prominence which appears to have been given to the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) in some of the news broadcasts Which are made, because I fully realize that the more prominence which is given to the hon. member and his party and the policies of that party, the more clearly will the people realize what they would come [DOT]to if that party should by chance ever come into power.
He complains of the "soap programmes". What will happen if his party should come into power? Not only would the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation become publicly owned and publicly operated, but all the private chains and stations in this country would be taken over, and not only the soap advertising but the "baloney" advertising as well would be paid for by the people of this country through the licence fees which they pay. Let me say to him that our people are not so gullible as all that. So that the more prominence tlhat is given to Mr. Coldwell and the policies of the party he represents, the more it will work to their detriment and to the advantage of the system' which is in vogue in this dominion at the present time.
I am sure that all realize that radio is a vital organ in Canada's national life, and the people are convinced of the soundness of the policy of publicly owned radio as an instrument of education, information and entertain-

ment. Above all, in war time no greater instrument of building up and sustaining public morale exists.
It is very easy to criticize. While we are making that criticism, would it not be well if we had some knowledge of the accomplishments of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? I think it can be fairly said that the corporation has a fine record of accomplishments in the last six or eight years. Radio coverage has been extended from 46 to 92-4 per cent of the population. Four high-powered stations have been completed across Canada. Interference from United States and Mexican stations has been limited by wise agreements. Programmes have been most materially improved and extended by fostering native talent and securing the best programmes from the United States and Great Britain. Since we last met, a new type of news service has been inaugurated. The C.B.C. subscribes and pays for a news service which is supplied by the Canadian Press and the British United Press. That has given greater coverage. More particularly, the corporation's contribution to war publicity in every phase has been outstanding and has formed a valuable link between the soldiers, overseas and their relatives at home. In addition, we have with the armed forces at the present time in Italy, as we had in Africa, a mobile unit -which has operated continuously throughout the different theatres of war.
In addition to these achievements, since the last report was given to parliament there has been started the building of a short-wave station. Also another network, known as the Canadian network, has been established.
These, Mr. Speaker, are achievements which the Canadian people ought to know of, and I am sure that they have accrued to the benefit of the listening public throughout Canada.
Criticism has been made with reference to the directorate. That directorate has been considerably strengthened. The directors who have been added are Mr. Chase, Mr. Parker and Mr. Crawford. These men are outstanding in their particular lines of endeavour or of business; they are men who enjoy the confidence of the people who know them, and who bring to the directorate years of experience and good judgment.
It is true that the position of general manager has been vacant, as such, for a number of months. There cannot be any great criticism in that particular regard. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) says that that has brought about chaos in the direction of the management. There is nothing at all, in my judgment, which would

Radio Broadcasting Committee
indicate that there has been chaos of any kind with reference to the management of the C.B.C. The assistant general manager, Doctor Frigon, stepped up to the position-temporarily-as general manager of the corporation. There is not a man on the North American continent who has greater technical knowledge of radio than has Doctor Frigon. I submit that the direction of the management of the corporation has actually been bettered by stepping up Doctor Frigon to that position than if a new man had been appointed to it.
With reference to the managerial set-up, I believe the time has come when it would be advisable to have a full-time, well-paid general manager of the corporation, a man who would have the same rank as a deputy minister and would have under him a general manager who would be his executive head. In that event it would probably be possible to have a much smaller directorate. I realize very well the difficulties there are in this country with reference to a directorate of such an organization as the C.B.C. Canada's geographical position, the various national aspects and, if you wish, religious aspects of the undertaking, and other considerations make it extremely difficult to secure a directorate which will work in harmony all the time. Since the last report of the committee, the directorate have been meeting much more frequently than they formerly did. Meetings are held every two months, but I would suggest that if there were a smaller board of governors it might be well to have regional advisers for the four different sections of the country, the mari-times, Quebec, Ontario and western Canada. We could easily have managerial or regional advisers in these four sections who would give the benefit of their experience, and they would probably be much more conversant with the problems that confront radio management in their own particular sections.
Let us, however, face the facts. There will never be a radio set-up in this country which will entirely satisfy all sections. In the very nature of things that is not possible, because there is such a diversified interest in the public. One part of the public wants sports; another part wants music; another part wants some kind of intellectual lectures, and when they turn on the radio and do not get the particular programme which they like they think the radio is to be condemned for that reason. We have to cater to a great population with a diversified interest, and as long as the national system is making an attempt to cater to that diversified population, with its various tastes, we cannot please all at the same time. That might just as well be borne in mind when there is criticism of the corporation.
Some mention has been made of the amount of commercial work which is carried on by the organization; I mean the fees which are collected from industry for advertising purposes. It was never contended, as has been stated in some of the newspapers of the country, that the C.B.C. could carry on entirely on licence fees collected from the public. It was always thought there would have to be some revenue from commercial advertising. It has been said that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was originally constituted on the altruistic basis recommended by the Aird commission, that all revenues which the publicly-owned corporation required were to be provided by the licence fees. Mr. Morin, chairman of the board of governors, answering a criticism by a newspaper in this country in that regard, has this to say:
This statement, though completely erroneous, has been circulated so assiduously and continuously by critics of the corporation and especially among the newspapers, that many who have never consulted the record have come to believe it. The Aird report says definitely: "It is rather difficult to estimate what revenue would be collected for the rental of time, but we think that an amount of approximately $700,000 annually could be expcted at the beginning." Note, the Aird commission says "at the beginning", which indicates clearly that the commissioners expected this sum to increase from year to year.
The second error has to do with the revenues of the C.B.C. from advertising. It was stated as $1,800,000 a year in 1943. As a matter of fact, that is exactly $500,000 or nearly forty per cent more than the estimated revenue for 1943-44, which is $1,300,000. Then Mr. Morin goes on:
Even this revenue, however, is not net. There are numerous items which must be deducted from it to obtain a net figure to the corporation. Moreover, it includes a very substantial volume of governmental war advertising which is obligatory and transitory.
That is to say, when the C.B.C. do a certain amount of advertising for the government they are paid for it and that is business which they cannot loolj to continuously from year to year, so that it is of a transitory type which the organization cannot count on.
If all these are considered it will be- found that C.B.C. revenues from commercial broadcasting even after several years of operation do not greatly exceed the figures originally set in 1928 by the Aird commission. There is no enormous jump in advertising revenues as suggested.
I see no harm in the C.B.C. getting a certain amount of revenue from advertising. All organizations having to do with broadcasting in the United States are privately owned and obtain their entire revenue from commercial

Radio Broadcasting Committee
advertising, and the revenue of some of these organizations is very high. That of the national Broadcasting Company is $80,000,000 a year, and that has something to do with the type of programmes we are bound to have. Any organization that has a revenue of $80,000,000 a year and a population of 130,000,000 from whom talent can be drawn is in a much better position to give programmes that are considered better than those we are able to provide in this country.
What we want to do is to build up in Canada a type of programme that will be indicative of our Canadian people and Canadian culture, and it is folly to think we can have programmes put over the C.B.C. network that will compete with those in a country in which bigger organizations with much more money to spend are operating.
It has also been said that there is conflict between the C.B.C. and the privately owned stations. I do not think anything could be farther from the facts. The C.B.C. and the privately owned stations are made to appear as competitors, implying beyond question that there is unfair competition and disaffection among the privately owned stations. The facts are anything but as represented in that type of statement. The relationship between the C.B.C. and the privately owned stations is one of cooperation, not competition. Of the eighty-nine private stations that are on the air, seventy are on one or other of the C.B.C. networks and share in the revenues from network advertising, and they share on a very fair and equitable basis. They receive every day many programmes which they could not otherwise broadcast and which listeners in many parts of the country could not hear were it not for the C.B.C. network programmes which enhance the prestige and greatly increase the audiences of the privately owned stations.
I submit that were it not for the C.B.C. with their two extensive networks across the country, the manner in which they feed the privately owned stations with programmes, and the contribution they make to the revenues of those stations by passing on advertising to them, these privately owned and operated stations could not exist. It is because of that fact, because they are willing to cooperate with this great national and publicly owned utility, that the relationship between the privately owned station and the nationally owned station is as harmonious as it is.
In conclusion, I see a great future for radio in Canada. Let us remember that it is only in its infancy. I hope that the government will continue to maintain it as a strong public
[Mr. McCann.J
utility and a great instrument for education, information and entertainment. I hope that the committee, which is about to be set up, will give the affairs of the corporation earnest and sincere consideration and will make without fear or favour such recommendations as are considered to be in the interests of this public utility of the Canadian people.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
I should like to support the hon. member who has just taken his seat; but in the words of another we might well say that "the half has not been told". I have appreciated the work of the. Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in many ways. We have fun for the children; we have beautiful swing music for the young people and the help in the home, and we have relaxation for those like ourselves who have a good deal to think about when we can turn on the radio and listen to the broad-east of a hockey match. If we turn down the lights we can visualize ourselves witnessing a really thrilling game.
But that is not what I want to speak about. I should like to say, in support of the management of the C.B.C., that they are doing a great job in putting on "The Church of the Air" on Sunday afternoons. That halfhour on Sunday afternoons is better than all the rest that is put on the air on Sunday. It gives a colour that is badly needed to the citizens of Canada. Not only that but "The Church of the Air" on Sunday afternoons does two things. It permits the citizens of Canada to hear the best clergymen of the dominion, and those who listen in to "The Church of the Air" can go back and tell their own minister that he compares favourably with the best doctors of divinity in Canada.
I should like to pay my tribute to the local broadcasting stations. We are permitted to have a devotional period over our local station nearly every morning in the week, and they do not charge us five cents for it. Anybody who would not appreciate that is extremely stingy. I was one of those who tried to help along that line, and I have received more letters because of that than I ever received from giving a political speech over the radio. Therefore I say that the management have the right to be supported in giving leadership of a kind that is badly needed all over Canada, in allowing each of the denominations to have its turn on the air, to enlighten the citizens of Canada and to tell them of the Master Workman whom if they will follow, they will never come to grief.

Radio Broadcasting Committee

It is not my intention to delay the passing of the resolution to set up the committee; but before the motion is put to a vote I should like to suggest to the minister under whose department the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation comes, that they should be furnished with more powerful stations, stations that can send the message over the air for a greater distance than any of the stations we have in Canada can now send them.
In the Yukon we are not very far away from Vancouver, or Edmonton or any of those northwest cities. But in our locality it is seldom, if ever, that we can get any sound of a Canadian broadcast. speechtext: No. If the work of the corporation is to be effective in Canada it should have better equipment. Something has been said about the commercialization of the C.B.C. subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER ANNUAL REPORT AND REVIEW POLICIES OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Some of the remarks and speeches made this afternoon impel me to rise in my place and say a word or two regarding some of these before the resolution is passed.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), in speaking about publicity, pointed out something each and every hon. member knows and fully realizes, namely, that speeches made in this house against either the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) or the C.C.F. have the effect of giving him or them lots of publicity; and they have had lots of publicity so far this year, due to that very method being applied. The hon. member for York South
who, by the way, is one of the newer members of the house, may think he is letting the members of the house into a secret. Let me say to him in all sincerity that he is entirely wrong. Many of us have realized for a number of years that the more you attack a person or a party, the more you are publicizing that individual or party and making them better known to the world. I just wish to disillusion his mind in that respect and to tell him that many of us are fully aware of that. Three years ago the viewpoint was held by many members of the C.C.F. party that their speeches and debates in the house had the members of parliament buffaloed, but at least some members of that party have changed their minds in that respect, because they have realized this year that there are members on this side of the house who can hold their own when it comes to debating. I point that out in passing, because I should not like the impression to go abroad that the members on this side of the house are a lot of greenhorns; they are not.	.
Some references were made to the fear that some of us hadi of turning all radio over to the C.B.C.; that we were somewhat afraid of democracy. That is not an entirely true interpretation of the views which many of us hold. May I say that I am one of many other hon. members who fear a government monopolistic concern, just as much as we fear a private monopolistic concern. There is just as much danger in one as there is in the other, for this reason: we are nine provinces, and I view with some alarm much of the centralization that has taken place in Ottawa since the war commenced. Perhaps I speak as one who comes from three thousand miles away and who views with alarm this centralization; yet I say to the hon. members, let us be very careful and watchful of this government monopolistic concern. We know not what the future may hold; but, if not properly controlled or adjusted, it may be just as evil an any private * monopolistic concern could be.
I have a great deal of sympathy for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, because, to my mind, they have done a great work. I do not think, however the entire picture has been put before the house this afternoon. I rather suspect the C.C.F. realize to a greater extent what the act actually contains than do some other hon. members. I was one who sat in the house in 1932 when the first radio bill was passed. I was more susceptible in those days than I am to-day, and I fell for things much more readily than I do now. I must admit that I was somewhat carried away by the statement of the then Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, who
Radio Broadcasting Committee

painted a wonderful picture of what the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation would be for this country. He had in mind something which is still incorporated within the powers of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, but which is not generally understood, namely, the idea that there would be no private stations, once the corporation could operate fully.
There are those in the house who believe that everything in this country should he government-owned or state-owned. I differ from those views, and especially as it applies to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It was pointed out in 1932 and has been pointed out since that radio in Great Britain is entirely government-owned. The statement was made further that in the United States, our neighbour to the south of us, it was entirely pri va tely-o wned.
I am one who believes we should follow neither country. This country is entirely different from the United States. We are a country of only some twelve million people. The latest report I have from Great Britain is -and it might be well for the committee to look into this-that the people over there are just waiting for the end of the war so that they can throw overboard their government-controlled radio. That is the information I have. Let us not be too easily carried away with the thought that as a part of the commonwealth we in this country might very well follow along the lines of Great Britain. I say to members of the house, and to the committee to be set up: Let us have our own system, one peculiar to this country of ours, following neither the one in Great Britain nor that in the United States.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), I believe by way of interjection, compared the radio with the two railway companies to-day. That is just the idea I should like to see carried out, a radio -system somewhat similar to the two railway companies, one privately owned and the other government-owned, with a body supervising both. While there has been a good deal of criticism against private ownership by those who say, "criticism is just an attempt by the privately owned radio stations to throw the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation overboard," the information I have is that the owners of private radio stations have nothing but praise for the government-owned corporation. They realize, however, that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is working under difficulties, and that those difficulties are contained within the very act under which it works.
The owners of private radio stations do not want the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to be done away with. And while we give praise to the C.B.C. we must also give praise to the private stations, because it must be remembered that they were in existence long before the C.B.C. came into the picture. They would be in a better position to-day, were it not for the fact that they are circumscribed by the rules and regulations laid down by the C.B.C., the object of which in 1932, and I think in 1936 when the bill was put through, was gradually to have all radio absorbed under government ownership.
That thought and that information has'not been put before members of the house, and I am taking a few minutes time just to place it clearly before them, believing that the act itself should be changed, and also that there is a place in this country for both privately owned and government-owned stations. If that change is not made, and privately owned stations are put out of business, we might have a serious monopolistic state-owned concern which none of us would like, and for which the country would suffer.	*
Information is given to me that on account of this very fact Canada's position will be very weak in 1946 when the conference is held at Havana, because the lines in this country have not been fully and properly developed. As is well known, the privately owned stations are held down to not over 1,000 watts. We in British Columbia can very well complain about the discrimination we suffer because, while Toronto and Montreal under the C.B.C. have 50,000 watt stations, there is no such station, or no station of that power in British Columbia. I bring this matter to the attention of the committee, and would ask that they give it consideration.
Something has been said about freedom of the air. I draw to the attention of the committee that there is some danger of allowing too many newspapers or newspaper chains to own and control private radio stations. In that lies a danger. A short time ago exPremier Pattulo of British Columbia introduced a measure which, I understand, has been refused by the legislature, under which he would compel newspapers to print letters sent to them in self-defence by those who have felt that they have been defamed through either editorials or letters sent to the newspapers concerned. Nothing so far, I believe, has been done about that bill, but it has some merit. It does show, however, the trend of things, and that matters of this kind will have to be considered. I would ask the committee to view that aspect- of our radio set-up, and find
[Mr. Reid.J

Radio Broadcasting Committee
out how many newspapers are in control of private radio stations. More than one newspaper has taken the attitude, and so stated, that it was in control of many of the public men in this country and, by criticism, could put some of them out of public life. I, for one, do not want to see freedom of speech, either through the medium of the press or over the air, put into the hands of private monopoly, nor do I wish to see freedom of speech over the air put completely under a government monopoly, such as we are drifting to in this country.
Hon. L. R. LaFLECHE (Minister of National War Services): Mr. Speaker, this afternoon and this evening I listened to some excellent and constructive criticisms, and to others which, to my mind, were to the contrary. First, I shall say a few words, not about that which is constructive, but in answer to some of the allegations which have been made in this honourable house.
Before proceeding to do so, may I observe that we in Canada have in operation a dual system of radio broadcasting. We have a system which last year I described in the following words-words which I believe still describe the situation prevailing in Canada:
In the matter of radio broadcasting as in so many other respects, Canada occupies a midway position between Great Britain and the United States. In Great Britain, broadcasting is controlled by the crown, whereas in the United States, radio is privately owned. In Canada we have both systems and I have not yet observed anything which has convinced me that we should be better off with either one or the other system alone. It is a matter for serious consideration whether it were wise to make up our minds in regard to this matter whilst Canada is engaged in war, or even until some time after the war is over, until victory is won, and we are well advanced in the reconstruction work which must necessarily follow this war.
I make the further observation that Canada is still engaged in a life or death struggle with her enemies. The flower of our young manhood and womanhood are fighting our enemies thousands of miles away from their homes. It might not be fair to those who have undertaken the great responsibilities of defending us so that we may live safely in peace at home to decide certain problems before they are able to return to this country. War time is not a normal time. Situations are aggravated in times of war. I am really stating my personal belief that we would do well to make haste slowly in deciding finally whether Canada is to adopt one of these two systems or whether we should try to do better with what we have.
It is possible to do better with what we have. That applies not only to our radio 100-57
broadcasting system but to every other human endeavour. It is our. purpose in life to progress, to do better with those things which we control. It was with real regret that I heard to-day what sounded to me like reflections upon those Canadian citizens, all persons of standing and quality, who have assumed the onerous duties of membership on the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It is indeed poor recompense to be criticized in a place where they have no voice.

But the board of governors have not yet made a recommendation to me in regard to the general manager. I know on good authority that the board of governors have been able to operate very successfully even though there has been one missing, No. 9. It must be remembered that the radio broadcasting act provides for the automatic filling of the position of general manager when he is absent. Therefore, there has been at all times a general manager of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Section 6 of the act makes the provision I have in mind in regard to the appointment of a. general manager of the corporation. It says that the general manager shall be named by the governor m council on the recommendation of the board of governors of the C.B.C.

I know the board of governors have been giving extremely careful attention to this matter. They have wanted to make a recommendation to me, but they have not yet done so, and until they do I am quite powerless to take any action in the matter. I have heard something said in the house to-day about commercial advertising on the radio and it seemed to be in the mind of some hon. gentlemen that the C.B.C. has entered upon a field where it has no right. I do not believe that is the case. I have read the act again, and paragraph (f) of the objects of the corporation will relieve any hon. member's mind as to its being quite within the intended objects of the corporation to enter into contracts here in Canada or elsewhere in connection with programmes.
In view of what I have brought to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the position of the corporation has become weakened, it has been suggested, in the minds of the Canadian public, which is something that I do not admit or believe. But were such the case, I am very sorry to have to say that in my opinion such weakened position, such impaired reputation of the corporaton, would be due to those who have thoughtlessly or for other reasons spoken so often to the public in that vein. They themselves are responsible. In that connection I would say this. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a valuable piece of property. That piece of property belongs to the people of this country, and I submit that it is a piece of property the value of which should be safeguarded by all Canadians. I think all hon. members have a direct and specific duty in helping to preserve the value of that piece of property. I know of no better way of protecting that property than by each of us in this house doing what he can to preserve and enhance the reputation of those who are there doing the work.
So far as the board of governors are concerned, they are working for nothing, and again I bring that to your attention, Mr. Speaker, and to that of hon. members because I know that in the final issue this house is a very fair-minded body of men. Until we win a victorious peace, the main objective of our lives to-day, I should so much like to see in Canada some of that peace-loving here at home for which our boys are fighting so far away from us.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT TO COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REFERENCE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I would ask leave to return to the order for motions. We have now appointed all the committees. In other years there has been a suggestion that the auditor general's report and the public accounts should be referred to the public accounts committee at an early stage of the session. I would therefore move:
That the public accounts for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1943, and the auditor general's report for the year 1942-43 he referred to the standing committee on public accounts.
Motion agreed to.
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Bradette in the chair.
1. Departmental administration, $130,406.

There are two matters I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture. While neither of them may come directly under his administration, still I cannot see how the procedure I am about to discuss could become effective unless through the advice of his officials, or of the minister himself.
The first item has to do with the cost of hay. In British Columbia the ceiling price on hay amounts to some $22 a ton. May I point out that I thought it was foolish to put a ceiling price on hay because, as is well known, hay is one commodity which is exchanged between farmer and farmer, and does not as a rule travel any great distance from one market to another.
What is the present situation in regard to hay in British Columbia, and particularly at points along the Pacific coast? It is maintained that the ceiling price is away below the cost of production. Many farmers have taken the attitude that they are not going to sell a product, the cost of which has been far more than would be the selling price. The result is that hay has not moved, and that there is a shortage in certain districts. I understand hay is being brought in from the prairie provinces, and that $35 to $39 a ton is being paid. Usually straw is sold for half the price of hay. However, the situation on the Pacific coast, and in the Fraser valley is that in many instances straw is being sold for $24 or $25 a ton, whereas the selling price of hay, no matter what the quality, is set at $22.
That is the situation faced by the farmers in that area, and it is a condition which is affecting purchasers of hay. I suppose the wartime prices and trade board officials have discussed this matter with officials of the Department of Agriculture. But if they did I am wondering if they took into consideration the extent of the country, and that the fixing of a ceiling price at one point may work a hardship and have no bearing whatsoever on actual conditions in another.
The other point to which I would direct the attention of the minister has to do with potatoes. The treaty on potatoes allows potatoes from the United States to enter free. But, generally speaking, all potatoes going to the United States have a duty placed upon them. We in British Columbia have been
Supply-Agriculture

developing a seed potato market, and it is estimated that there are about a thousand tons of first-class seed potatoes available and for sale, for which a ready market can be found in the state of Washington. But when those potatoes are exported to Washington, those purchasing the seed have to pay a duty of $15 a ton on which, to keep the record straight, I believe they have a rebate of $7.50 a ton after six months. But in effect the price given by the Washington buyers of seed to the sellers of seed potatoes in British Columbia is set, with that tariff to be paid in lieu.
I am one who believes in reciprocity. If we allow potatoes to come into this country free, then they should allow our potatoes to go into the state of Washington, or into other states free. I do not know how this situation affects the farmers of the maritime provinces, but I know the potato situation is greatly affected in British Columbia, on account of the tariff condition.
I believe these regulations are set, first of all, by the Minister of Finance, under the trade treaties, and, second, by the wartime prices and trade board, in so far as the question of hay is concerned. But I am beseeching the minister to do something about these matters. On many occasions I have said I should like to have seen the minister in charge of these matters, because I do not think the injustices and inequalities prevalent in agriculture would have been so marked, had all agricultural matters been under his control.
Since these matters have been drawn to my attention, and because they affect our people greatly, I am asking the minister to make a statement. If he has not the information at hand, I am asking if he will present the matter to his departmental officials, and to the wartime prices arid trade board.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
This is a matter under the control of the prices board and I have not before me the details with which to deal fully with it. From what has been said by the hon. member for New Westminster I understand that farmers in his district find it difficult to carry on trading in hay as between farmers in the same area, because certain price ceilings have been placed on that commodity.
I am not sufficiently familiar with the regulations with regard to hay to deal with the matter to-night, but I shall bring down this information when my estimates are up at a later time.
I should think there is some argument for maintaining that where a transaction is between farmers in a district it should be pretty well taken care of as it is in connec-

tion with most other commodities upon which the price board has placed control. I understand why ceiling prices are necessary in order to maintain controls when hay is delivered to a market, or when it is shipped from one part of the country to another, but as a rule the transfer of a commodity from one farmer to another within a district is pretty well taken care of. This principle is generally applied in connection with the ceilings placed upon different products.
What about potatoes?

They are under the control of either the customs or the prices board, and I would not care to offer an opinion at the moment without getting further information from them.
I have before me a statement in answer to some of the questions asked the other evening by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) and having to do with grass seeds, particularly clover seed and alfalfa seed. I think I should put these answers upon the record at this time. Under authority of order in council, P.C. 5428, dated July 9, 1943, the special products board was authorized to purchase and to become the sole exporter of surpluses of agricultural seeds, subject to determination by the Minister of Agriculture as to classes of seed to be included. The board was also authorized to arrange for the distribution to producers of each class of seed of any net profits resulting from its transactions. The reasons for the establishment of this method of control were set forth in the order in council as follows:
That prices for certain agricultural seeds used only for seeding purposes obtainable in the United States and other allied countries are considerably higher than prices obtainable in Canada under established price ceilings;
That these differences in price have rendered it impossible to control exports in a manner equitable to producers and at the same time to assure retention and distribution in Canada of supplies of seed necessary to meet domestic requirements;
That to secure for producers the full advantage of export outlets for such seeds and to secure equitable allocation of supplies to allied nations which are looking to Canada as a sdurce of supply of these seeds, it is necessary to centralize all export transactions.
In other words, all seed purchased is purchased by the board and distributed to the different allies. Up to the present time it has been found necessary to make the special products board the sole exporting agency for only the following classes of seeds: alfalfa, alsike, red clover and alsike-white clover mixtures. Subject to the securing of export permits on the recommendation of the agri-

Supply-Agriculture
cultural supplies board, the seed trade or producer cooperatives have been free to take advantage of any export outlet available for seeds such as sweet clover, timothy and brome grass, production of which in 1943 was greatly in excess of Canadian requirements.
Purchase by the special products board of alfalfa, red clover, alsike and alsike-white clover mixtures has been limited to quantities surplus to Canadian requirements and to supplies required, as in the case of alfalfa, to meet allocations by the combined food board to the United Kingdom. Seeds required to meet Canadian requirements are handled as in the past through regular seed trade channels.
Prices at which the board has been prepared to purchase any of the seeds brought under its control were set forth at the beginning of the season in detail by grades on an f.a.s. Halifax basis, and at levels in relation to established retail ceilings which should permit seed needed to meet Canadian requirements to move freely. These prices are materially below those available not only in the United States but in the United Kingdom at which seed exported by the board will be sold.
Net profits to the board from its transactions resulting from the difference between the prices at which seed is bought by the board and resold by it, less any cost of moving the seed other than the administrative costs of the seed export office, will be returned to producers who sold their seed on a participation plan. In other words, producers will receive in full measure any profit resulting from export sales uninfluenced by the operations of speculative interests. The value to producers of participation certificates issued for any kind of seed sold by them will be dependent upon the amount of seed of that kind exported and upon the total quantity of that kind of seed purchased by the trade on a participation basis from farmers up to March 15. That is the total statement in answer to the questions asked the other evening by the hon. member for Melfort.

The hon. member for Melfort wished to know whether or not those who are purchasing seeds on participation certificates have been instructed to issue certificates to those from whom they purchase. It seems that some farmers who have sold seeds to these purchasers did not receive participation certificates, and they had no assurance that they would participate in the profits obtained from the sale of the seed.

When the statement is read in Hansard I think it will be found that it is made quite clear. There is a possibility that seed may be sold without its being placed 100-58
in the hands of the board, and of course in such cases there would be no participation certificate. A man may make a deal with another person who desires to buy seed and he will probably not ask for a participation certificate. If he desires to deal through the board, or if the board is purchasing for export, then participation certificates will be asked for and obtained.
Who is doing the purchasing for the board?
Any of the approved seed houses.
If purchases are made by persons not operating seed houses they would not have to give participation certificates?
The term "seed dealer" would cover practically any person in the habit of purchasing seed from farmers and selling it to others. Such a dealer would issue a participation certificate.

I understand the war distribution board of the United States are now taking a great many cars of potatoes off their market in order to support the floor under potatoes and that our wartime food corporation is bringing those potatoes into Canada to supply our market when there is a surplus of potatoes in this country. Can the minister tell me how many cars have been purchased in the last few days by the wartime prices and trade board and how many they intend to bring into Canada?

I am sure my hon. friend will realize that it would not be possible
for me to have information here as to the number of cars purchased within the last few days. That information is not available. I would suggest to the committee that these detailed questions about individual items should be asked when we reach the particular items, and then we could carry on any general discussion we wish to have from where we left off last Friday.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister is quite right. There was to be a general discussion on this item, and questions on the details of individual items should be asked when the items are reached.

When I asked my question a
few moments ago I could not find an item in the estimates on which I could ask about the exportation of potatoes, nor did I see any item on which I could ask about hay prices. That is why I brought those two questions up now. I said that in British Columbia there

Supply-Agriculture

were about a thousand tons of first-class seed potatoes available and for sale. I particularly mention that because the committee will remember that last year I had an argument with the minister and some of his officials who had said that the Fraser valley was a deficiency area so far as .potatoes were concerned. I pointed out then that the Fraser valley could grow any amount of potatoes, and this year the Fraser valley producers saved the situation in Ontario, because twelve care of good British Columbia potatoes were sent to Ontario from there not long ago, but for which the potato situation in Ontario would have been very short indeed. We are anxious that the minister will make representations soon regarding the exportation of seed.

The question might have been asked under the item relating to fruits and vegetables. I give the only answer I could give to the question asked a few moments ago, because it really does not touch this department at all. I just made a general statement with regard to it. I think we should discuss details about individual items as they are reached.
If too many potatoes come into our market they will demoralize the market. It is up to the minister to protect the market on agricultural products.

The minister has made a statement regarding the seed situation and regarding the remarks made by the hon. member for Melfort. I think the minister's answer was fairly complete, but as I understand it the hon. member for Yorkton asked about participation certificates and whether they had been handed out to everyone who had sold seed. In my area a certain amount of seed had passed out of the hands of farmers before this order came down, and for that reason they did not receive participation certificates. I think what the hon. member for Yorkton had in mind to ask was whether these gentlemen who had sold their seed prior to the bringing down of the order which the minister read are going to receive participation certificates. I believe it is true that they did receive a higher price than that received after the order came down.
I would ask the minister to explain to the committee, just why the special products marketing board set the price for the seed for export at the levels they did. It certainly is not in line with the retail ceiling price which we can get for seeds in Canada; setting the price they did on red clover, alfalfa and alsike had the effect of bringing down the price to the farmer, and as a result the seed that was sold in the domestic trade is going to give a

handsome profit to the dealer. If I understand the situation there will be little, if any, alfalfa to be shipped out of the country and no red clover at all. So that the participation certificates will not be of any value on these two classes of seed. On the other hand, there will be 'quite a handsome profit on alsike seed. These participation certificates will be worth a considerable amount. The primary dealers bought the seed first from the farmers, cleaned it once and resold it, and the result will be that the farmers are going to say, when the proceeds of a big participation certificate are returned to them, that the dealers have not paid them enough. They are going to say: We have been gypped for years past by those dealers. I do not think it is fair to the dealers that they should be blamed. I would ask the minister to explain, if not now, on some other item just why the special products marketing board placed these prices where they did. In my opinion they were not high enough.

I probably misled the
committee in bringing down this answer at all at this time. The question was asked the other evening and I passed it over then. The discussion properly comes under item 19 relating to plant products, seeds, feeds and so forth.
Or else under the item: for the special products marketing board in the war appropriation.

Either one or the other. There were two or three statements made by the hon. member for Melfort the other evening which covered the points raised and now I have specific answers for them which I should like to place on the record. For example, it was stated by the hon. member for Melfort:
This year, the special products marketing board has taken over the complete marketing of grass and clover seed, all domestic requirements being handled through that board.
That is his statement. Now here are the facts: Up to the present time	the board	hasnot been handling all	clover	seeds	as,	forexample, sweet clover, has not taken over the sole export .of any grass seeds, and has not been authorized to handle seed for domestic requirements.	The	board	is	nothandling much of the	seed.	Much	of	the
seed is being handled by seed houses and others, unless it is being purchased for special purposes. Not all of the different kinds of grass and clover seeds are being handled by the board.
The next statement was this:
According to a return tabled yesterday on the motion of the hon. member for York East (Mr. McGregor), the export price is 314 cents a pound.

Supply-Agriculture
That is the statement already on Hansard, made by the hon. member for Melfort. The answer to that is: This is the price at which the board is purchasing registered No. 1 alfalfa, f,a.s. Halifax. The price at which this seed will be resold to the British ministry of agriculture will be materially higher. Therefore there will be a further distribution to persons with participation certifications.
Another statement made was this:
However, I do not see why the producer of alfalfa seed should bear the brunt of this action. He is facing a loss of from 8 to 10 cents a pound.
That was the statement made the other evening. The answer to that is this:	As
stated, any profits resulting from export transactions in respect to any class of seed handled by the board will be returned to producers who sold on a participation basis seed of that class ultimately used either in meeting domestic requirements or in filling export orders.
Those are the facts with regard to the matters discussed the other evening. If the committee is agreeable, I should like to have further discussion of seed matters take place when the officials are here with all the facts.

I fully agree with the minister and will make only one further remark now, and that is in the nature of a warning. This other item might not come up before a considerable time. If I am correctly informed, there is not enough alfalfa seed in Canada this year to meet our domestic requirements. It would be too bad if seed were exported from the country by the special products marketing board or any other organization and not enough seed left in the country to go around. That is particularly true of eastern Canada. We must get our supplies from the west this year. I hope the minister will take these facts into account before any damage is done.

That is the objective of the order in council which was passed last year. By the sixth of July there could not have been much seed exported out of last year's crop. The intention is to do the same as is now suggested ought to be done, namely, to take control over the export of seed to see that too much does not go out of the country.
Some has gone out?
Yes.

When the agriculture estimates were being discussed last week and again this evening, we covered western agriculture fairly well, and got into Ontario and back to British 100-584
Columbia. This evening, perhaps, we should be able to start east and work west, east being the cradle of agriculture in this Canada of ours.
These lands that I wish to speak about were growing excellent crops when the buffalo and the Indian still inhabited the western plains. In any event, we have the sun in our backs instead of in our eyes, as some of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation from the west must think when they come to our province from time to time, and try to convince those of our farmers who are chafing to some extent under controls made necessary by the war, that in the socialistic state which they advocate the farmer will not be regimented, but can continue as a free enterprise individualist as he is at present. That was all I had to say to my hon. friends from the west. We certainly appreciate what they are up against in their agricultural problems, and we wish them well.
What I desire to speak about more particularly this evening is our marshland problem in Nova Scotia. I do not know whether this is the proper item under which to discuss it. Will the minister say if it comes under some other item?

The proper place to discuss it is under "specials," I would say, the rehabilitation vote, if there is any place to discuss it here. The suggestion is that rehabilitation activities should be extended to all parts of Canada, and that kind of discussion of course would come up in connection with "specials," the last items in the estimate.
What is the number?
Number 29.
The minister will be able to give us some information on that item concerning this problem, what was done last year and if anything is proposed to be done this year?
I think I could give now all the information under the general discussion, that could be given at any time. It is not really any item in these estimates.
That is what I thought. I thought we could discuss it at the present time.
Does the hon. member desire the information now?

I had a few remarks which I should like to make at some time. There came to my desk this morning, as I think there came to the desk of all hon. members, a pamphlet regarding the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act entitled, "A Record of Achieve-
Supply-Agriculture

ment", and I certainly agree that it is a record
of achievement of which the present government may be proud, in taking these dried-out areas from relief and converting them into productive areas. On page 13 of this pamphlet is a picture of a very extreme case, a group of buildings almost completely covered by sand. I admit that it is a dreary picture, but I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, and to this committee that it is no drearier than to see hundreds, yes, thousands, of acres of land which produced crops for many years now covered twice a day by the tides of the bay of Fundy; and that is exactly what is taking place in the maritime provinces, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
I know this problem has been before the authorities for some time. A small survey was made last year, but no actual work has taken place. I believe the suggestion was made that this was a provincial problem, or a municipal problem, but not a federal problem. On the other hand, if I understand correctly the operations of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, it is carried out entirely by the federal government. As is known to hon. members, the situation with respect to the maritime farm lands was studied by the committee on rehabilitation and reestablishment, and in two of their reports they have referred specifically to the situation. They recommended the extension of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to cover eastern Canada. That is what we from eastern Canada are looking for, because we feel that our farmers need some assistance along the general lines of this act.
I could refer to other measures which have been passed specifically to assist western agriculturists. As I said before, we have no quarrel with that policy. In addition to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, there is the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, the Wheat Acreage Reduction Act, and the prairie farm income regulations, all of which seem to have been aimed specifically at the western provinces, while eastern agriculturists have been left pretty much on their own. Now we are hopeful that, with the rehabilitation programme before us, we can see some constructive steps taken for the relief of our marshland problems and other agricultural problems in the maritime provinces.
I happened to be at one of our municipal council meetings this fall before I came to Ottawa. People were appearing before the council asking for reduction of taxes to almost nothing, because their dike lands had gone back to the sea and they were not in a position to build up the dikes again. The problem is now too big for the individual; there must be some other organization behind

us; and it seems to me that in that respect the federal government has an excellent chance of being of some real assistance to our farmers.
Would the hon. member tell us how many acres are affected and why that result has come about? I am much interested.

The acreage, or at least the amount of marshland, is somewhere 'between one hundred and fifty and two hundred thousand acres. The condition which we are in now has been brought about very gradually, by the operation of the tides wearing into the dikes, and the waters carrying them out. It has probably come to a head more in the last few years on account of the great shortage of man-power. Men are not available to repair the dikes, and even if they were, I question if at the present rate of wages the farmers could afford to hire them. The marshland has been gradually going back. One piece of dike would1 break out and would flood a hundred or two hundred acres this year, and then more the next.

When were the dikes
built?

The original dikes were built somewhere between 1600 and 1755, the time the Acadians were settling in the country. They were built by the French settlers and kept up by hand by the individual farmers right down through the generations. With the loss of our hay market, the result of losing to a large extent the export market in cattle to the old country, the farmers lost heart in the marshes and did not take the same interest in the work. Then there was the labour situation. The hand labour used to build the dikes fifty or sixty years ago has gone entirely. I was going to suggest in the meantime that prior to some general plan, if some temporary assistance could be given our farmers in repairing their dikes, through the use of machinery at low cost, perhaps in cooperation with the provincial government, perhaps in cooperation with the various defence forces, a large number of suitable machines in the adjoining areas, which for some reason or other cannot be obtained by the farmers, could be utilized to assist them in throwing up temporary dikes. This would save the situation and prevent further inroads by the sea until such time as a general plan could be worked out. I would commend to the minister some temporary arrangement whereby these temporary works could be undertaken to prevent further breaking of the dikes and prevent further land from being flooded. I wmuld strongly urge that a study be made of the

Supply-Agriculture
machinery necessary to make the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act apply to all eastern Canada. I know that the introduction of such a measure would meet with approval from all sides of the house as far as private members are concerned; at least, that is the impression I get. It might meet with opposition from certain sections from the treasury benches, but I am looking to the Minister of Agriculture to overcome that.

The problems confronting the farmers are so many and varied that in discussing them a person finds himself apt to get from one department to another. I have no wish to go beyond the Department of Agriculture, because I feel that the minister has enough to answer for without having to bother with the sins of omission and commission of some of the other ministers. When the estimates were last under consideration some hon. members had something to say about the expenses of the Minister of Agriculture and also of his department. The minister seemed ready to go to any length to show that he was not very much concerned about the matter. In fact, he appeared to be rather proud of it. I quote from page 673 of Hansard of February 18, where he is reported to have said:
That is the only explanation I wish to make in connection with the expense accounts, so far as my own expense account is concerned. Incidentally, it has been throughout those whole eight years one of the highest expense accounts among ministers of the government, and I am rather proud of that fact.
To me it seems a good deal like whistling in. the dark. I think the minister was more concerned about it than he tried to let on, and for that reason I intend to make a suggestion to him this evening. I suggest that when the minister finds it necessary on some future occasion to pay a visit to Humboldt constituency he should let me know. If he does I shall be pleased to make all the necessary arrangements for transportation and I shall see that he gets around the constituency. In that way I suggest he will be able to save a good deal on the cost of tires and the use of that famous car which last year carried licence number 20456, about which we heard so much.
What some of us are interested to know is whether the minister also used that car to go to Selkirk to look around in his official capacity.
I did not. I can answer that right away.
Or did he have another car at his disposal there?
That is the time he went over the ditch.

There are some people in Humboldt who were quite concerned when they heard that a certain car had met with a slight mishap because they were afraid that the country might have to get along for a while without a minister of agriculture. I can assure the minister that if he accepts my invitation I will drive with a great deal more care and see that he does not land in the ditch, because the policies of our Minister of Agriculture have so nearly run so many of us into the ditch that we do not want the hon. gentleman to go into the ditch along with them.
In connection with expense accounts the minister said, as reported on the same page:
Having said that, may I add that there is no inspector in the Department of Agriculture who is inspecting agricultural activities throughout the rural areas who would be worth his salt if he did not have a high expense account.
I have found that in the Department of Agriculture there are some very fine and able men, some men who do their jobs and do them well. There are in the various branches of the department inspectors who are really inspectors and who do get around and attend to their work. But I am very much afraid that too many of the inspectors in some of the departments under the Minister of Agriculture have heard him say, or had some reason to believe, that he was proud of their large expense accounts. I know of different cases that I could relate from now to midnight, but we do not want to sit so late to-night. I could tell of inspectors who seemed deliberately to run up big expense accounts. Let me mention one instance. I know of an inspector under the P.F.R.A. who had six or seven dug-outs to inspect in one locality. He landed there between three and four o'clock in the afternoon and inspected one dug-out. He asked that man where the other five or six were- I forget whether there were six or seven altogether in the neighbourhood-and this man said, "There is one over there, another over there, and I have a couple of hours to spare, so that I can go around with you and we can have them all checked now." Oh, no; he was sorry, but he could not take advantage of that man's kindness. He had to be back in Humboldt at a certain time and somewhere else later on. That inspector made a separate trip into that neighbourhood to inspect every one of those dug-out locations. He was certainly trying to be worth his salt. And there are other inspectors I have known who have carried on in such a way that they accumulated enough salt

I have mentioned the P.F.R.A. I will now give another example under the P.F.A.A. An inspector stopped along the road inspecting for the dried-out bonus. I happened to be broken down with a combine alongside the road and I was trying to repair it in a hurry. This chap came along and started talking, wanting to know about this and that. Finally I looked at him and said: "Are you another one of those inspectors running around here?" He said, "Oh, yes, I am supposed to be inspecting these dried^out areas." I said, "There is the field; look it over." He said, "I am not supposed to go any farther than three hundred feet. Do you think that crop will bring twelve bushels to the acre?" I looked at him and said, "Friend, it will be just too bad for me if it does not bring more." He said, "It won't bring more than twelve bushels to the acre." I said, "I have not time to argue with you. Go out and take a look." He stayed around for half an hour talking. He said, "What do you think it will bring?" I said, "If I could make one round with this combine I would be able to give you a far nearer estimate. At the present time, I do not know." I am telling you, Mr. Chairman, the grain that we were standing in there at that time was very good. If the whole field had been like that it would have brought between thirty-five and forty bushels to the acre, and that chap was asking me if it would bring twelve. I made the first round after he had gone, after I had got the combine fixed. By the time I had the hopper filled and placed in the box I said to the chap with me, "This grain is running somewhere around twenty-four bushels to the acre at the present time." Later on, it thinned out a little bit, but it averaged somewhere around twenty-two bushels to the acre, and this chap was standing there wondering whether it would run twelve bushels to the acre.
That inspector was as useless as the fifth wheel on a wagon. He had no more idea what that crop or anybody else's crop would bring than a child. Furthermore, that year we were required by law or regulation, after our harvesting operations were over, to report to our elevator where we were making our deliveries and to give an affidavit as to the number of bushels that we had threshed. That being the case, what was the need for the inspector and others like him running around the neighborhood?
I come now to the W.A.R. I may say that the first time I had any experience with

the W.A.R. was in the city of Regina when the first wheat acreage reduction bonus was on. I went there to attend a provincial session. I had a whole flock of letters from different people around the country with me, complaints about their wheat acreage reduction bonus. Finally I located the office. It consisted of a whole floor in one building. I said to myself, this is quite a good-sized establishment. They should be able to handle this. A day or two afterwards I found they had another whole floor taken up with offices somewhere else. Was there turmoil in those offices? The reports that were sent in by most of the inspectors were enough to turn anything into a turmoil. I met some of my colleagues at the buildings. They said, "Where were you; you should have been at a caucus this morning?" I said, "I was in a war office." They said, "Where is that?" I said, "Down there on a certain street in the city. It is war." I remarked that the way these fellows are going about their work we shall have a war before we get the bonus, and things straightened out. There were men running through the province drawing salaries and building up these handsome expense accounts who did not do anything else but make a heap of trouble for the people.
I admit there were some who were good and who tried to do their best.
Most of them were good.

After a whole lot of them were cleaned out, most of them were all right.
I say it was a disgrace, when you think of the men who came out there and the amount of useless time and effort they put in on a lot of that stuff.
There is one more point I should like to ' take up with the minister. I hope he does not take it too seriously because he has been used to it for a long time.
Not at all.

The minister made a statement a week ago that I was surprised to hear.
I thought he was just pulling off a nice little joke when he made the reference to which I am referring. I shall quote a part of his statement which is found at page 676 of Hansard. He said:
I know there are fellows who live outside large cities like Winnipeg who pride themselves upon being farmers, but they spend most ot their time in Winnipeg sitting on boards of one kind or another.
First of all, I think a man who has had the experience of the minister and who has served the length of time he has in parliament and in public life would have had a little more consideration for a new member, but he used

Privilege-Mr. Coldwell
the language I have just quoted in connection with my colleague. I think he simply could not overcome the temptation to use that little paragraph. After thinking it over more seriously I have come to the conclusion that in an unguarded moment when the opportunity arose to use that little crack the truth came out. The policies of his department and of the government have been for years that we farmers should stay out on the farm and do the slugging and grubbing and let the other fellows run our business. For too long we have let armchair farmers and swivel-necked politicians run our business. The time has come for us to do more along the line of that which the hon. member for Selkirk was doing, take an active part in our affairs and have something to say in what is going on.
I noticed throughout the evening while the discussion was going on in regard to these estimates that practically every hon. member on the government side of the house failed to recognize the main point that the hon. member for York ton made when he was delivering his speech, namely, that while we are prepared to admit, and no sensible person will deny that at the present time as far as the farmers are concerned they are receiving more money for most of their products than they have for a long time, the hon. member for Yorkton was pointing out something which is undeniably true, namely, that for all these years we have been so far below parity that you can go out into the homes and on the farms of the farmers and you will find that it will take a whole lot more than one or two years of fair prices before these people can get anywhere near to what they are entitled.
I believe it was the hon. member for Qu'Appelle who said that he did not believe in going around knocking. I agree with him; yet at the present time it is necessary for us to face facts. There is no person in his right senses who can say that just because we have had one or two years in which we have been receiving-in fact it is not even two years, it is not even one year-anywhere near a suitable price for our wheat, everything is all right. But admitting that, in one or two years you cannot erase the past ten or twelve years that the farmers have faced. It will take quite a number of years of decent prices for us to be able to say that now the farmers are enjoying that security to which they are entitled.
I would urge the minister in all fairness and sincerity to look upon those farmers who are doing the farming as men who are prepared also to do their share for the welfare of our country. I say that the farmers are becoming
more and more concerned about what is to be done, and they are going out to see that it is done.
